texts.text: Methods: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized control trials that evaluated the efficacy of maternal RSV immunization against infections in infants, as well as the efficacy of RSV vaccines in older adults. The primary outcome was the vaccine efficacy against RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD). Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation criteria was used to evaluate the level of evidence.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Results: Ten trials were included in the review. For maternal vaccination, the RSV vaccine showed favourable efficacy against RSV-related LRTD (vaccine efficacy 57.3%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 31.373.5; low certainty) and RSV-related severe LRTD (vaccine efficacy 81.9%, 95% CI 56.8-92.4; moderate certainty) in infants within 90 days after birth. For older adults, Meta-analysis showed that RSV vaccines could also reduce the risk of RSV-related LRTD (vaccine efficacy 78.3%, 95% CI 65.6-86.3; moderate certainty) and RSV-related severe LRTD (vaccine efficacy 86.5%, 95% CI 68.3-94.3; moderate certainty). There was no significant difference in serious adverse events between RSV vaccines and placebo.

texts.orig: Efforts to develop a vaccine for RSV have indeed remained highly active despite the initial setback in the 1960s with the formalin-inactivated RSV vaccine [1]. Currently, there are numerous RSV prevention candidates in clinical development utilizing six different approaches: recombinant vector, subunit, particle-based, live attenuated, chimeric and nucleic acid vaccines [6]. These diverse approaches reflect ongoing research and commitment to finding an effective and safe RSV vaccine. In recent years, significant progress has been made in the development of RSV vaccines. Arexvy (RSVPreF3) became the first RSV vaccine to receive approval from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in May 2023 [7]. It is specifically approved for the prevention of LRTD caused by RSV in individuals aged 60 years and older. Additionally, in August 2023, the FDA approved Abrysvo (RSVpreF), which is the first vaccine authorized for use in pregnant women to prevent LRTD and severe LRTD caused by RSV in infants from birth through 6 months of age [8]. However, it's worth noting that not all RSV vaccine candidates have shown efficacy in clinical trials. Two trials evaluating RSV vaccines in adults aged 60 years or older, one based on RSV postfusion F protein and the other utilizing a nanoparticle-based RSV-F vaccine, did not demonstrate protection against RSV-related illness [9 , 10]. The synthesis of evidence regarding RSV vaccines for the prevention of infections in infants and older adults is indeed urgent and necessary. It is crucial to assess the potential benefits and risks of RSV vaccines in these vulnerable populations. Therefore, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of phase 2/3 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to determine the efficacy and safety of RSV vaccines in infants and older adults.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We conducted this meta-analysis according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [11], and the protocol was registered on PROSPERO. We searched for literature published on PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library and grey literature from the ClinicalTrials.gov website until 1 September 2023. If a trial is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov but does not have any available results, it is common practice to search for additional data related to the study on other platforms, such as searching on Google. Keywords including 'respiratory syncytial virus', 'RSV', 'vaccine', 'vaccination', 'immunization' and 'randomized control trial' were used to search, and the detailed search strategy was shown in the Supplementary material. Additionally, we identified references by searching the reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews. Considering that the researches on RSV vaccines were updated quickly, we researched the literature before submission on December 15, 2023.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We included phase 2/3 RCTs evaluating the efficacy of RSV vaccines in target populations (maternal vaccination to protect against infections in infants, and adults aged 60 or older), irrespective of RSV vaccine type, control group or length of follow-up. We excluded phase 1/2 trials that did not report vaccine efficacy. Additionally, study protocols, editorials, comments, reviews, conference abstracts, ongoing trials and studies without sufficient data for analysis were also excluded from our review. The primary outcome was the vaccine efficacy against RSV-related LRTD depending on the definition of trials. Secondary outcomes included vaccine efficacy against RSV-related ARI, RSV-related severe LRTD and hospitalization for RSV-related LRTD. Safety outcomes, such as any adverse events (AEs) and serious AEs (SAEs), were also considered as part of the secondary outcomes. AEs and SAEs were defined according to the definitions of each included study.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Two authors reviewed titles and abstracts independently to identify eligible studies that met pre-specified inclusion criteria and extracted data. When consensus was lacking, a third reviewer was consulted. Study characteristics (e.g. journal and year of publication, study design, sample size and length of follow-up), intervention and comparator characteristics (e.g. type of vaccine, manufacturer and status), participant characteristics (e.g. age and sex), and outcomes were extracted. RSV-related LRTD with at least 3 symptoms was regarded as RSV-related severe LRTD. The risk of bias of RCTs was assessed by the Cochrane Collaboration's tool (RoB 2) [12], which includes the following domains: randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. The quality of evidence for each outcome was evaluated with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework [13].

texts.orig: Data synthesis and analysis
texts.text: Data synthesis and analysis

texts.label: text
texts.orig:
Initially, we conducted a narrative descriptive synthesis to evaluate the vaccine efficacy and safety of the included RCTs. Based on their developmental status, the vaccines were categorized into three groups: approved vaccines, promising vaccines in the approval process, and failed or discontinued vaccines. Approved vaccines are those that have received market approval from regulatory authorities. Promising vaccines are those showing favourable results in the approval process. Discontinued vaccines are those that manufacturers have announced will no longer be developed or marketed. Only approved and promising vaccines were included in our quantitative analysis to evaluate the potential benefits and risks of RSV vaccines that are more likely to be available for use in the foreseeable future. The two target populations, infants and older adults were analysed separately. We conducted DerSimonian and Laird random-effects meta-analysis when data were available for at least two studies [14]. Data were analysed as relative risk or absolute risk with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Vaccine efficacy was defined as (1 − relative risk) × 100%. Statistical heterogeneity between the studies was assessed with the χ 2 test and the I
2 statistics. I
2 values of 25%, 50% and 75% have been suggested to be indicators of low, moderate and high heterogeneity, respectively [15]. All the analysis were performed with Stata 17.

texts.orig: Three trials [17 , 18 , 22] reported the efficacy of RSV vaccination during pregnancy to protect against infections in infants. Two trials [17 , 22] were conducted on RSVpreF, and one trial [18] was conducted on RSV F vaccine. The relative risk for RSV-related LRTD, RSV-related severe LRTD, and hospitalization for RSV-related LRTD appeared to be lower for RSVpreF compared to RSV F vaccine, both at 90 and 180 days (Figure S1). Noted that the reported vaccine efficacy of one phase 2b trial of RSVpreF in infants was based on exploratory, post hoc analyses [22], which might cause bias. Therefore, only one trial [17] was included to evaluate the potential benefits of the RSV vaccine (RSVpreF). The RSV vaccine showed favourable efficacy against RSV-related LRTD (vaccine efficacy 57.3%, 95% CI 31.3-73.5; absolute risk, 92 fewer per 10,000 patients, 95% CI 42-142; low certainty), RSV-related severe LRTD (vaccine efficacy 81.9%, 95% CI 56.8-92.4; absolute risk, 78 fewer per 10,000 patients, 95% CI 43-113; moderate certainty) and hospitalization for RSV-related LRTD (vaccine efficacy 67.9%, 95% CI 34.684.2; absolute risk, 60 fewer per 10,000 patients, 95% CI 25-96; low certainty) within 90 days after birth. The RSV vaccine efficacy was slightly lower at 180 days after birth compared to the efficacy observed at 90 days, as shown in Table 2 .

texts.orig: Three trials [17 , 18 , 22] involving two vaccines, the RSV F vaccine and RSVpreF, reported any AEs and SAEs in both maternal and infant participants (Figure S3). texts.label: text
texts.orig: This systematic review and meta-analysis included 10 RCTs involving 12,400 pregnant women, 12,102 infants and 115,653 older adults. The primary objective was to provide a comprehensive overview of the efficacy and safety of RSV vaccines. Among the six vaccines included, only one will be used for pregnant women to prevent RSV infection in infants, and three of them will likely be used for older adults. The findings revealed that the RSV vaccine (RSVpreF) demonstrated positive outcomes in infants. Specifically, per 10,000 participants, the vaccine was associated with a decrease of 92 cases of RSV-related LRTD, 78 cases of RSV-related severe LRTD, and 60 cases of hospitalization for RSV-related LRTD within 90 days after birth. Regarding older adults, the RSV vaccines also showed promising results. Per 10,000 older adults, the vaccine was associated with a decrease of 22 cases of RSV-related LRTD, 35 cases of RSV-related ARI and 9 cases of RSV-related severe LRTD during the first RSV season following vaccination. Furthermore, no significant difference in SAEs was observed compared to the placebo group.

texts.orig: To our knowledge, our study is the first comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis to characterize the efficacy and safety of RSV vaccines. A recent review provided an overview of RSV vaccines under clinical development, highlighting various target populations, antigens and trial outcomes [6]. The review indicated that most vaccines included in the analysis demonstrated safety and good tolerability based on phase 1/2 trials. However, some crucial phase 3 trial results were not available in that review. Similar findings were reported in a previous review that specifically examined the immunogenicity and safety of RSV vaccines under development [26]. Differences in efficacy were observed between approved vaccines and those that did not meet the desired outcomes, which could be attributed to variations in their development approaches. Two approved vaccines, RSVpreF and RSVPreF3 OA, are based on the RSV prefusion F protein. The promising vaccine, mRNA-1345, encoding the stabilized RSV prefusion F glycoprotein, utilizes a nucleic acid approach. However, the discontinued vaccine (Ad26.RSV.preF) employed a recombinant vector strategy. The two vaccines that failed, RSV F vaccine and MEDI7510, were an RSV F nanoparticle vaccine and a postfusion F protein-based vaccine, respectively.

texts.orig: RSV-related LRTD poses a significant burden of illness and mortality among young infants worldwide, particularly in low- and middle-income countries [27]. Recently, nirsevimab, a monoclonal antibody, has been authorized for use in infants from birth during the RSV season based on three clinical trials [28-30]. Infants who received nirsevimab injection were protected from RSVrelated LRTD for up to 150 days after the injection, demonstrating an efficacy of 74.5% (95% CI, 49.6-87.1) [28]. This efficacy appears to be slightly higher than that of RSVpreF vaccine, which demonstrated an efficacy of 52.5% (95% CI, 28.7-68.9) within 150 days af- ter birth [22]. However, further evidence is needed to determine the true comparative effectiveness between the two interventions. Additionally, the affordability and cost-effectiveness of these interventions in low- and middle-income countries remain uncertain. Data from low-income countries where the vaccine is likely to have the greatest effect is limited for RSVpreF in infants [17]. Although the trial of RSV F vaccine was not powered to evaluate vaccine efficacy according to country income level, it appeared that the vaccine efficacy against RSV-related LRTD in infants was greater in low- or middle-income countries compared to high-income countries [18]. It is important to note that the efficacy and safety of RSV vaccines in preterm infants are not yet known. Additional studies are needed to determine if the variation in vaccine efficacy in infants between high-income and low- or middle-income countries is a consistent finding. Furthermore, the effectiveness of maternal RSV vaccination in preventing RSV-related LRTD in preterm infants should also be evaluated in the future.

texts.orig: This review has several strengths. First, the systematic review and meta-analysis followed the PRISMA guidelines and had a protocol registered in PROSPERO. We searched multiple databases comprehensively and included all available RCTs that reported the RSV vaccine efficacy. Second, the risk of bias for included trials was assessed using a valid methodological tool, and the quality of evidence for each outcome was evaluated using GRADE. Third, we have performed sufficient analysis in the review. A narrative descriptive synthesis was conducted for all included RSV vaccines to provide a comprehensive overview of their characteristics, efficacy and safety. However, only approved and promising vaccines were included to provide more precise quantitative data to inform decision-making and better understand the potential benefits and risks associated with these vaccines.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We also acknowledge some limitations. First, the limited number of enrolled trials is a result of the ongoing development of RSV vaccines. We could only include one trial for infants and three trials for older adults to evaluate the potential benefits of RSV vaccines. Second, it is important to note that a significant number of phase 1/2 trials only provided data on the safety and immunogenicity of the vaccines, which were not included in our analysis. This limitation may reduce the statistical power of our safety analysis since we did not have access to the complete safety data from these trials. Third, the effectiveness and safety of RSV vaccines in real-world settings remain unknown, and further studies are needed to address this gap. Fourth, the results of this meta-analysis may not apply to certain clinically relevant subgroups, such as preterm infants and frail older adults. Finally, due to the limited number of included trials, we were unable to perform subgroup analyses on vaccine efficacy against specific RSV subtypes (A and B) or evaluate vaccine efficacy in different age groups.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In conclusion, this systematic review and meta-analysis indicate that RSV vaccinations could offer protection against RSV disease in older adults as well as infants if administered during pregnancy, without apparent safety concerns. However, further evidence from real-world settings is necessary to strengthen these findings and evaluate the vaccine effectiveness in broader populations. Additionally, assessing the cost-effectiveness of RSV vaccines compared to monoclonal antibodies is crucial, considering factors such as efficacy, safety, duration of protection and overall economic impact. This information will be valuable for decision-making and resource allocation in RSV prevention strategies.
